Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two separate sets of entities. These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. We demonstrate that deciding whether a planar drawing is achievable by splitting at most $k$ vertices is fixed parameter tractable with respect to $k$. Furthermore, assuming the standard complexity theory that $P\neq NP$, we prove that this optimization problem is not fixed parameter tractable when considered against the size of the graph. Finally, we apply these findings to assess the feasibility of achieving planarity through the splitting of one or two vertices. Additionally, the approach described here may benefit visual comparison techniques used in sports analytics. Such comparisons often involve a feasibility matrix displayed as a heatmap, which can be replaced by a bipartite graph. Since sports teams are frequently evaluated on multiple factors, visual comparisons of feasibility between teams and their potential competitions can be achieved through a "feasibility tree," a method proposed and analyzed in [3]. Such comparisons can now be made laterally between a bipartite graph and its corresponding feasibility tree. Lastly, the results of this study could assist in assessing the limitations of all-pairs shortest paths graphs when used for multi-criteria optimization.
